# Unclaimed

The rule at the depot is ninety days. Anything found on a train or a platform comes to the property room, gets tagged and logged in a ledger older than me, and waits three months for its owner to come back. If nobody comes, it goes to auction — a folding table in the maintenance bay where men in fleece vests bid four dollars on electric razors.

I have worked the property room for eleven years. People imagine it's full of umbrellas, and it is — umbrellas the way the ocean is full of fish — but umbrellas are the least of it. People leave their lives on trains. They stand up too fast, thinking about the meeting, the argument, the funeral, and they walk off without the thing beside them, and the thing rides on alone to the end of the line.

Some of what comes through is exactly what you'd expect: phones, laptops, groceries, a prosthetic leg (twice; different legs). Some of it is stranger. A mannequin torso. A sealed aquarium, fish still alive, which we kept fed until a man claimed it on day eighty-eight and thanked us like we'd been babysitting his children. A cake, once — sheet-sized, frosted CONGRATULATIONS DEREK — riding six stops before anyone noticed Derek was not aboard.

A wedding dress came through in my fourth year, garment-bagged, tags still on. Somebody bought it, boxed it, carried it onto a train, and then — what? Cold feet on the Green Line? We never learn the endings. The dress sold at auction for forty dollars to a woman whose daughter was marrying in June and, she said, couldn't be picky. I choose to believe that's true.

Then there are the things that arrive quiet and stay quiet.

There's a box of letters, postmarked 1974 through 1981, all addressed to the same man, none of them sent — no stamps, no address, just his name on the front like a prayer. A woman wrote him every week for seven years and kept every one. Her handwriting goes from careful to hurried to shaky. The last letter is dated nine days before the postmarks stop. We ran the name. He died in 1996. She may still be alive. The letters sit in drawer C, long past their ninety days, because nobody has the heart to lay them on the auction table between the rice cooker and the crate of Beanie Babies.

There's the urn. Small, brass, heavy as a hammer. Found on the 6:40 express, seat 14A. We called every funeral home in the county. We put it in the paper's lost column, which felt obscene and necessary both at once. Nobody came. That was four years ago. The state says ashes are property, same as anything else, and property has a shelf life. I moved it from the shelf to my desk instead. It sits beside my stapler. Some mornings I say good morning to it. I don't know whose it is. I hope that wherever they were headed, somebody was there to meet them.

Here is what eleven years teaches you: almost nothing is truly lost. *Lost* implies a failure to find. Most of this was set down. There's a difference. You set down your mother's ring when you pull off your gloves, and you stand up, and the doors close, and the ring continues north without you, and for two days it isn't lost — it's just somewhere you aren't yet. Grief works like that too, I think. Things get set down. It doesn't mean they're gone.

People do come back. That's the part nobody believes. A woman returned eight months past her deadline for a canvas bag holding her father's tool belt, and when I told her it had gone to auction she said, "Oh," in a voice like a door closing, and then, "He was wearing it when he died." I broke about six regulations and bought it back from the auctioneer for twelve dollars. She cried in the parking lot. So did I, later, alone in the property room, which smells of raincoats and old gum and which I have come to think of as the most honest room in the city — everything in it abandoned mid-thought.

And I'll confess one more thing, since we're here.

In my second year, a kid's notebook came through. Spiral-bound, a dinosaur on the cover. Inside, a story in pencil, ten pages, about a knight who was afraid of dragons and went on the quest anyway. Spelling everywhere. The last page read: *THE END?* And beneath it, smaller: *i dont know how he beats the dragon.*

No name. No school. Day ninety-one came and went.

It's in my bag right now. It has been in my bag for nine years. I am not a thief. I tell myself I'm holding it in trust — that someday a grown man will wander in saying he lost a notebook when he was nine, and I'll hand it over, and he'll laugh, and he'll go home and finish the story. Statistically, this will not happen. I know that. But somebody wrote those pages, and somebody's hand shook a little writing them, and it seemed wrong — it still seems wrong — for the only copy of a person to end up bid on by men in fleece vests.

So that's the job. You hold things for people who are coming back, and you hold things for people who aren't, and mostly you can't tell the difference, so you hold everything, gently, for ninety days, and then you decide what deserves longer.

The urn gets good morning. The letters get dusted. The notebook gets carried.

And every day the trains run, and every day somebody stands up too fast, thinking about something else, and leaves a piece of themselves behind — and every day it arrives at my window, damp from the rain, warm from somebody's lap, waiting to be missed.

Some of what comes through is exactly what you'd expect: phones, laptops, groceries, a prosthetic leg (twice; different legs). Some of it is stranger. A mannequin torso. A sealed aquarium, fish still alive, which we kept fed until someone claimed it on day eighty-eight and thanked us like we'd babysat his children. A cake, once, sheet-sized, frosted CONGRATULATIONS DEREK, riding the Red Line for six stops before anyone noticed Derek was not aboard.

Then there are the things that arrive quiet and stay quiet.

There's a box of letters, postmarked 1974 through 1981, all addressed to the same man, none of them sent — no stamps, no addresses, just his name on the front like a prayer. A woman wrote him every week for seven years and kept them all. Her handwriting goes from careful to hurried to shaky. The last letter is dated nine days before the postmarks stop. We ran the name. He died in 1996. She may still be alive. The letters sit in drawer C, past their ninety days, because no one has the heart to put them on the auction table between the rice cooker and the crate of Beanie Babies.

There's the urn. Small, brass, heavy as a hammer. Found on the 6:40 express, seat 14A. We called every funeral home in the county. We put it in the newspaper's lost column, which felt obscene and necessary. Nobody came. It's been four years. The state says ashes are property, same as anything else, and property has a shelf life. I moved it from the shelf to my desk years ago. It sits next to my stapler. Sometimes I say good morning to it. I don't know whose it is. I hope wherever they were going, somebody met them.

Here's what eleven years teaches you: almost nothing is truly lost. Lost implies a failure to find. Most of this stuff was set down. There's a difference. You set down your mother's ring when you take off your gloves, and you stand up, and the train doors close, and the ring continues north without you, and for two days it isn't lost — it's just somewhere you aren't yet. Grief works like that too, I think. Things get set down. It doesn't mean they're gone.

People do come back. That's the part nobody believes. A woman returned eight months after the deadline for a canvas bag containing her father's tool belt, and when I told her it had gone to auction she said, "Oh," in a voice like a door closing, and then, "He was wearing it when he died," and I broke about six regulations and bought it back from the auction guy for twelve dollars. She cried in the parking lot. So did I, later, in the property room, which smells like raincoats and old gum and which I have come to think of as the most honest room in the city — everything in it abandoned mid-thought.

And I'll confess one more thing, since we're here.

In my second year, a kid's notebook came through. Spiral-bound, dinosaur on the cover. Inside, a story written in pencil, ten pages, about a knight who was afraid of dragons and did the quest anyway. Spelling everywhere. The last page said: THE END? and under it, smaller: i dont know how he beats the dragon.

No name. No school. Day ninety-one came and went.

It's in my bag right now. It has been in my bag for nine years. I am not a thief. I tell myself I'm holding it in trust, that someday a grown man will wander in saying he lost a notebook when he was nine, and I'll hand it over and he'll laugh and finish the story. Statistically this will not happen. I know that. But somebody wrote those pages, and somebody's hands shook a little writing them, and it seemed wrong — it seems wrong — for the only copy of a person to end up bid on by men in fleece vests.

So that's the job. You hold things for people who are coming back, and you hold things for people who aren't, and mostly you can't tell the difference, so you hold everything, gently, for ninety days, and then you decide what deserves longer.

The urn gets good morning. The letters get dusted. The notebook gets carried.

And every day the trains run, and every day somebody stands up too fast, thinking about something else, and leaves a piece of themselves behind — and every day it arrives at my window, damp from the rain, warm from somebody's lap, waiting to be missed.
